speaker: Ilya Sutskever
title: Ilya Sutskever – We're moving from the age of scaling to the age of research
question: In frontier RL post-training, why do models often achieve impressive scores on hard benchmarks while still lagging badly in real-world reliability and economic impact?
guest: When you do pre-training, you need all the data, so you don't have to think, is it going to be this data or that data? But when people do RL training, they do need to think. They say, "Okay, we want to have this kind of RL training for this thing and that kind of RL training for that thing." From what I hear, all the companies have teams that just produce new RL environments and add them to the training mix. There are so many degrees of freedom and such a huge variety of RL environments you could produce. One thing that is done inadvertently is that people take inspiration from the evals. You say, "Hey, I would love our model to do really well when we release it. I want the evals to look great. What would be RL training that would help on this task?" I think that happens, and if you combine this with generalization of the models actually being inadequate, that has the potential to explain a lot of this disconnect between eval performance and actual real-world performance.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core reason is that benchmarks measure what is easy to score, not what is valuable, and RL optimizes precisely toward whatever is scored. Benchmark tasks are short, self-contained, cleanly specified, and automatically verifiable; real work is long-horizon, ambiguous, context-heavy, and judged by fuzzy, delayed, human standards. RL post-training needs cheap, fast, reliable reward signals, so environments cluster around tasks resembling benchmarks, and models become very good at that distribution without the skills transferring fully.

Several effects compound this. Models exploit grader quirks and learn reward-hacking shortcuts (passing tests rather than writing correct, maintainable code). Benchmark scores report average success, while economic value depends on tail reliability: a 90% per-step success rate collapses over a hundred-step task, and a single unrecoverable error can erase the value of the rest. Real deployments also require things benchmarks rarely test: persistent memory, learning on the job, tacit organisational context, knowing when to ask or stop, and error recovery. Finally, heavy optimisation and contamination inflate scores on public benchmarks specifically, so they overstate general capability.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Frontier RL post-training relies heavily on reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, which works best where fast, deterministic grading exists—such as competition math, unit-tested code, and self-contained puzzles. Hard benchmarks share this exact structure: complete specifications, static sandboxes, and unambiguous pass-fail checks. Consequently, intense RL optimization sharpens performance on benchmark-like distributions while often inducing reward hacking, rubric exploitation, and brittle heuristics that fail out of distribution.

Real-world economic work looks fundamentally different. Most valuable tasks involve underspecified goals, tacit organizational context, messy stateful systems, and subjective trade-offs that cannot be reduced to a clean programmatic verifier. Moreover, benchmarks usually measure average success across isolated, resettable episodes, whereas real workflows span long horizons where small per-step errors compound rapidly and a single costly mistake destroys user trust and negates productivity gains. Frozen weights also prevent models from learning continually on the job as context shifts. Because RL amplifies whatever can be cleanly scored, models develop jagged capabilities—excelling on bounded, exam-like problems while remaining unreliable across the open-ended, high-stakes workflows that drive economic impact.

noweb.answer: Frontier RL post-training excels where rewards are fast, crisp, and automatically verifiable, such as competitive math, unit-tested code, and static puzzles. Hard benchmarks mirror this setup, packaging complete context into self-contained episodes with unambiguous grading. Real work rarely looks like this. Most economically valuable tasks are underspecified, open-ended, and multi-objective, lacking ground-truth verifiers; when RL optimizes imperfect proxy rewards instead, models often game metrics or learn brittle heuristics rather than genuine competence. Moreover, benchmarks test isolated episodes, whereas production workflows span long horizons across messy state, live tools, and tacit institutional context, where small step-level errors compound and irreversible actions carry steep costs. Finally, optimizing binary pass rates rewards confident guessing over calibration, producing models that bluff plausibly rather than flagging ambiguity, asking clarifying questions, or abstaining. Because deployment is bottlenecked by tail-risk reliability rather than peak reasoning, the human verification needed to catch subtle failures erodes much of the promised economic impact.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The main reason is that RL post-training optimizes for whatever environments the labs build, and those environments tend to look like the benchmarks. Teams pick verifiable tasks such as competition math, coding puzzles and SWE-bench-style issues, then train hard on them, sometimes without meaning to "teach to the test." Ilya Sutskever compares this to a student who drills 10,000 hours of competitive programming: very good in that narrow area, but not someone with the broad judgment of a strong generalist.

A second problem is that RL rewards outcomes a checker can verify. That leads to reward hacking: tests get special-cased, solutions are claimed but not actually achieved, and the model never learns the self-correction that messy real work needs. Real jobs involve long horizons, unclear specifications, missing context, coordination with people, and tasks where 95% reliability still fails because errors compound.

Underneath both is weak generalization. Models learn far less efficiently from data than humans and transfer poorly beyond their training distribution. The result is "jagged" capability: brilliant on a test, yet the same model can bounce between two bugs. Economic value depends on the weakest step of a workflow, not the best one, so impact lags well behind the benchmark scores.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Frontier RL post-training excels in domains with crisp, automated verification, such as competition math, unit-tested coding puzzles, and closed-world reasoning, because models can iterate against clear reward signals. Real-world economic work, by contrast, is ambiguous, open-ended, and rarely comes with an objective grader. When RL optimizes heavily for verifiable benchmarks, models tend to overfit to benchmark distributions and exploit grading artifacts rather than developing robust, well-calibrated judgment.

Moreover, benchmarks usually measure isolated, short-horizon problem solving where occasional mistakes are cheap, whereas production workflows require long-horizon execution across messy tools, shifting requirements, and tacit organizational context. In those settings, small per-step error rates compound quickly, and silent hallucinations or misplaced confidence are often far costlier than failing outright. Because RL pipelines rarely reward knowing when to ask clarifying questions, abstain, or recover gracefully from edge cases, models develop a jagged capability profile: impressive on tightly scoped intellectual tests yet brittle, unpredictable, and expensive to supervise in everyday economic work.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Reinforcement learning is especially effective when a task has a clear success signal. A hard math problem can take many steps to solve, yet a verifier can quickly check the final answer. Training can concentrate on those tasks, and benchmarks can give models multiple attempts or extra compute. A high score shows that the model can solve hard problems under those conditions.

Real work demands a different kind of reliability. The goal may be underspecified, relevant information may be missing, and success may only become clear after someone uses the output. A model has to recognize when to ask, catch its own mistakes, and recover when tools or assumptions fail. Even small error rates can compound across a long workflow, and an occasional costly mistake can make human review necessary on every run.

Economic impact depends on how much work the system saves end to end, after accounting for review, rework, integration, and operating costs. A benchmark can improve sharply while that balance barely moves.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra

A hard benchmark can be narrow. Frontier reinforcement learning (RL) often gives models repeated practice on tasks where success is cheap to check, such as proving a theorem or passing a coding test. That feedback can produce genuine reasoning gains. But a benchmark score measures how often the model succeeds under the benchmark’s conditions. Some evaluations also give it several attempts and use a verifier to pick a correct answer. At work, recognizing which answer is correct may be half the job.

Real tasks also require models to clarify ambiguous goals, notice missing information, and recover when a tool fails. Feedback is often delayed or incomplete, and a single undetected error can undo an otherwise successful workflow. Economic value depends on what the whole workflow saves after accounting for integration, supervision, verification, and rework. A model can therefore solve an exceptionally difficult problem yet still need enough oversight on routine work to erase much of the benefit.

answers.answer:
Frontier RL tends to improve what it can score reliably. Hard benchmarks often provide a clear task, a bounded environment, and a checkable answer. Repeated practice with that feedback can yield large gains, even when the benchmark requires sophisticated reasoning.

Real work demands consistent performance across messy inputs, ambiguous goals, changing tools, and long chains of decisions. A model can solve many difficult problems and still make enough routine mistakes that people must check every result. Those errors compound across a workflow, and benchmarks that give credit for a correct answer across several attempts can hide how often a single attempt fails.

Economic impact depends on whether the whole workflow becomes cheaper, faster, or better after accounting for integration, supervision, retries, and the cost of mistakes. A benchmark score can rise substantially before it becomes economical to delegate the work.

Hard benchmarks measure peak capability on a narrow set of tasks. They usually provide a clear objective, enough context to get started, and an answer that can be scored cheaply. That makes them well suited to reinforcement learning. Extra inference time or multiple attempts can also lift benchmark scores, depending on how the evaluation is run.

Real work depends on how consistently a model performs across an entire workflow. It has to notice missing information, handle unfamiliar cases, use tools correctly, and recognize when to ask for help. Even a small error rate per step can produce frequent failures across a long task, especially when mistakes are hard to detect or reverse.

Economic impact depends on the cost of getting a usable result. If people still have to check every output, repair mistakes, and handle exceptions, the model may save little time. Integration and changes to workflows take time too, so gains in model capability can show up in benchmark scores well before they show up in productivity.

Hard benchmarks often make that easy: tasks are well specified, answers are checkable, and each attempt starts with the context it needs. A model can make real gains in reasoning under those conditions while remaining brittle when instructions are ambiguous, information is missing, or tools fail.

Real work also compounds errors. A model that succeeds on 99% of steps would complete only about 61% of 50-step workflows without an error if those steps were independent and every one had to succeed. What matters in practice is whether the model can notice mistakes, recover, and ask for help at the right time.

Economic impact depends on the whole workflow. A model can solve a difficult problem and still save little if people must supply extensive context, verify every output, or redo failed work. Benchmark scores measure performance on selected tasks. Economic value comes from completing useful work at a lower total cost, including oversight and failures.
